fixtures.competition_status_notes: Liga MX Apertura 2026: 18 clubs, single round-robin of 17 jornadas, compressed because of the 2026 World Cup; started July 16, regular phase ends Nov 22 (J17 Nov 20-22). Play-In was eliminated for this tournament: the top 8 go directly to the Liguilla. Quarterfinals: first legs Nov 25-26, second legs Nov 28-29 (higher seed hosts second leg; aggregate tie favours higher seed). Semifinals Dec 2-6, Final Dec 10/13 (or Dec 24/27 if Toluca qualifies, because of Toluca's FIFA Intercontinental Cup 'Derby of the Americas' in December). Rounds in the window: J11 Oct 9-11 (after the October FIFA window; Toluca away at Tigres, Fri Oct 9 21:00), J12 Oct 16-18, J13 midweek Oct 20-22, J14 Oct 23-25, J15 Oct 30-Nov 1, J16 Nov 6-8, J17 Nov 20-22 (after the November FIFA window Nov 9-17). Toluca's window fixtures: J11 at Tigres (Oct 9), J12 HOME vs Atlético San Luis (Sat Oct 17 18:00), J13 HOME vs Tijuana (Wed Oct 21, ~19:00 derived), J14 at León (Oct 24), J15 at América/Estadio Banorte (Oct 31), J16 HOME vs Monterrey (Sat Nov 7 19:05), J17 at Pachuca (Sat Nov 21 17:00). Toluca has no home match between Sept 29 and Oct 16. Pachuca (Estadio Hidalgo ~2,430 m, borderline venue): its only home match against a near-sea-level club, Pachuca vs Tijuana (J9), was played Sun Sept 20 at 18:00 – BEFORE the window; remaining Pachuca home games are Necaxa (Oct 11, 17:00), Cruz Azul (Oct 21, 21:00), Tigres (Oct 31, 17:00) and Toluca (Nov 21, 17:00), none from a near-sea-level base (Tigres/Monterrey ~540 m gives only ~1,890 m at Hidalgo), so no Pachuca borderline rows are listed; a Pachuca–Tijuana Liguilla tie is possible but Pachuca sat 11th (12 pts) after J10. Mazatlán FC NO LONGER EXISTS in Liga MX: the franchise was sold (Dec 2025 owners' assembly) and became Atlante (Mexico City, ~2,240 m) from Apertura 2026; Mazatlán's last home match was J16 Clausura 2026 (Apr 22). Dorados de Sinaloa (Liga de Expansión) now use Estadio El Encanto. Hence the only Liga MX visitor producing a >2,500 m gap at Toluca is Tijuana (Estadio Caliente ~20 m); Juárez (~1,140 m), Santos (~1,120 m), Monterrey/Tigres (~540 m) do not. Liga de Expansión MX Apertura 2026: no Toluca-based club and no matches at Nemesio Díez were found. Kickoff-time convention: Liga MX publishes provisional times in the pre-season calendar and confirms/adjusts jornada programmes ~1-2 weeks ahead; the J13 Toluca–Tijuana time (19:00) is derived from Pacific-time Xolos listings (18:00 PT) and a UTC-rendered tolucafc.com listing, not from a direct Central-time snippet, so re-verify. studies.title: Methods of the international study on soccer at altitude 3600 m (ISA3600)
studies.authors: Gore CJ, Aughey RJ, Bourdon PC, Garvican-Lewis LA, Soria R, Jimenez Claros JC, Sargent C, Roach GD, Buchheit M, Simpson BM, Hammond K, Kley M, Wachsmuth N, Pyne DB, Schmidt WF
studies.published_in: British Journal of Sports Medicine 47(Suppl 1):i80-i85; DOI 10.1136/bjsports-2013-092770; PMID 24282214
studies.population: Bolivian U20 club team (The Strongest, La Paz; altitude natives, n=19) and Australian U17 national team (Joeys; sea-level natives, n=20)
studies.altitude_range_m: 430 m (Santa Cruz) and 3,600 m (La Paz)
studies.design_and_measures: 3-year multinational project; five matches between the two teams (two near sea level at 430 m, three at 3,600 m on altitude days 1, 6 and 13); GPS match/training running, haemoglobin mass, blood volume, blood gases/acid-base, resting HR/HRV, Lake Louise AMS scores, HR and RPE to submaximal run, Yo-Yo IR1, 20 m sprint, actigraphy sleep
studies.measured_effects: Methods/overview paper; results are reported in the companion papers (Aughey, Buchheit, Wachsmuth, Sargent, Roach 2013; Buchheit 2015)
studies.limitations: Youth players (U17/U20), one camp, two teams only; all altitude matches were between the same two sides so opponent effects are confounded with acclimatisation day
studies.relevance_to_2500m_filter: Only controlled field dataset at 3,600 m (La Paz) with sea-level-native visitors; same venue class as the bettor's La Paz/El Alto/Potosí band; youth teams, so extrapolation to senior pros required

studies.title: Soccer activity profile of altitude versus sea-level natives during acclimatisation to 3600 m (ISA3600)
studies.authors: Aughey RJ, Hammond K, Varley MC, Schmidt WF, Bourdon PC, Buchheit M, Simpson B, Garvican-Lewis LA, Kley M, Soria R, Sargent C, Roach GD, Jimenez Claros JC, Wachsmuth N, Gore CJ
studies.published_in: British Journal of Sports Medicine 47(Suppl 1):i107-i113
studies.population: 20 sea-level-native (Australian U17) and 19 altitude-native (Bolivian U20) elite youth soccer players
studies.sample_size: 39 players; 5 matches (2 at 430 m, 3 at 3,600 m on days 1, 6, 13)
studies.design_and_measures: GPS match activity profile expressed per minute: total distance, low-velocity running (0.01-4.16 m/s), high-velocity running (HiVR, 4.17-10 m/s), maximal accelerations; peak 5-min period (D5peak, HiVR5peak) and subsequent 5-min stanza (D5sub, HiVR5sub) via rolling epochs; magnitude-based inferences
studies.measured_effects: Total distance per minute reduced by a small magnitude in the first match at altitude in BOTH teams, with no change in low-velocity running; HiVR per minute reduced at altitude in both teams (reviews of this paper describe 'moderate decreases in high-speed running distance' and 'large decreases in high-intensity intermittent running'); both teams showed substantial decrements in the 5-min stanza after the peak period (transient fatigue) in every match, with no substantial between-group differences in the altitude effect. Exact percentage reductions were not confirmed from search snippets.
studies.uncertainty: Magnitude-based inference (effect sizes with qualitative likelihood); numeric ES/CI values not confirmed from snippets
studies.limitations: Small samples; youth players; both teams played each other so match context varies; no senior professional data; time course limited to days 1, 6, 13
studies.relevance_to_2500m_filter: Direct evidence at 3,600 m that sea-level natives' high-velocity running falls on arrival; but altitude natives' running ALSO fell by a similar amount, so a running-distance gap between home and visiting team is not guaranteed; extrapolation from U17/U20 to pro clubs needed

studies.title: Wellness, fatigue and physical performance acclimatisation to a 2-week soccer camp at 3600 m (ISA3600)
studies.authors: Buchheit M, Simpson BM, Garvican-Lewis LA, Hammond K, Kley M, Schmidt WF, Aughey RJ, Soria R, Sargent C, Roach GD, Jimenez Claros JC, Wachsmuth N, Gore CJ, Bourdon PC
studies.published_in: British Journal of Sports Medicine 47(Suppl 1) (PMID 24282195; PMC3903314); page range not confirmed
studies.population: Sea-level-native (Australian U17) and altitude-native (Bolivian U20) young soccer players
studies.sample_size: ~20 Australians and ~19 Bolivians (ISA3600 cohort; exact n per measure not confirmed)
studies.design_and_measures: Daily on waking: body mass, resting SpO2, resting HR and HRV, perceived wellness questionnaire, Lake Louise AMS score; HR response to submaximal run; Yo-Yo IR1 and 20 m sprint near sea level and on altitude days 3 and 10; magnitude-based inferences
studies.measured_effects: On arrival Australians had moderate-to-large impairments in wellness and Yo-Yo IR1 relative to Bolivians; SpO2 'almost certainly' lower in Australians than Bolivians during week 1, difference progressively reduced from days 7-8 but Australian SpO2 still 'likely lower' at end of camp; acclimatisation of most measures substantially slower in Australians; only Bolivians returned to near sea-level Yo-Yo IR1 by end of camp; BOTH teams had moderately impaired 20 m sprint at end of camp. Conclusion: 2 weeks insufficient to restore physical performance in sea-level natives. Exact % decrements not confirmed from snippets.
studies.uncertainty: Magnitude-based inferences; numeric values not confirmed
studies.limitations: Youth players; no control group at sea level over the same period; single camp; training load during camp may itself have caused fatigue
studies.relevance_to_2500m_filter: Supports the premise that a sea-level visitor is still impaired at day 13-14 at 3,600 m (i.e., normal 1-3 day pre-match arrival gives no acclimatisation); extrapolation from youth to pros needed

studies.title: Changes in blood gas transport of altitude native soccer players near sea-level and sea-level native soccer players at altitude (ISA3600)
studies.authors: Wachsmuth N, Kley M, Spielvogel H, Aughey RJ, Gore CJ, Bourdon PC, Hammond K, Sargent C, Roach GD, Soria Sanchez R, Jimenez Claros JC, Schmidt WF, Garvican-Lewis LA
studies.published_in: British Journal of Sports Medicine 47(Suppl 1):i93-i99; DOI 10.1136/bjsports-2013-092761; PMID 24282216
studies.population: Sea-level-native Australian (n=20) and altitude-native Bolivian (n=19) soccer players
studies.altitude_range_m: 430 m vs 3,600 m; 13 days
studies.design_and_measures: Hb-O2 saturation, arterial O2 content (CaO2), haemoglobin mass (CO rebreathing), blood volume, blood gases before descent (Bolivians), near sea level, within 2 h of ascent and over 13 days at 3,600 m; Yo-Yo IR1 on altitude days 3 and 10
studies.measured_effects: Baseline [Hb] 18.2±1.0 g/dL and Hbmass 12.8±0.8 g/kg in Bolivians vs 15.0±0.9 g/dL and 11.6±0.7 g/kg in Australians; PaO2, Hb-sO2 and CaO2 of both teams fell within 2 h of arrival at 3,600 m (p<=0.001) then rose over following days; CaO2 overcompensated in Australians (+1.7±1.2 mL/100 mL, p<=0.001); blood volume fell ~400 mL in both teams; Yo-Yo IR1 lower on day 3 than day 10 and significantly related to CaO2. Authors state the marked drop in PaO2/CaO2 after ascent does not support a 'fly-in, fly-out' approach.
studies.uncertainty: p<=0.001 for arrival decreases in PaO2/Hb-sO2/CaO2; SD reported for CaO2 overcompensation; exact SpO2 values not confirmed
studies.limitations: Youth players; physiological rather than match outcome measures; no direct link to match result
studies.relevance_to_2500m_filter: Mechanistic support for immediate (within 2 h) oxygen-transport impairment on arrival at 3,600 m, which is exactly the fly-in-fly-out scenario typical of visiting clubs; fitness (Yo-Yo) tracked CaO2

studies.title: Relative Match Intensities at High Altitude in Highly-Trained Young Soccer Players (ISA3600)
studies.authors: Buchheit M, Hammond K, Bourdon PC, Simpson BM, Garvican-Lewis LA, Schmidt WF, Gore CJ, Aughey RJ
studies.published_in: Journal of Sports Science and Medicine 14(1):98-102; PMID 25729296; PMC4306790
studies.population: 7 sea-level-native (Australian U17 national team) and 6 altitude-native (Bolivian U18/U20 club) players with complete data
studies.design_and_measures: 10-Hz GPS distance >14.4 km/h and distance >80% of individual vYo-Yo IR1 (vYo-YoIR1 measured at sea level and altitude days 3 and 10); case report design
studies.measured_effects: On arrival at altitude, greater decrement in vYo-Yo IR1 and D>14.4 km/h in Australians than Bolivians; D>14.4 km/h fell in proportion to vYo-Yo IR1 in both groups so D>80%vYo-YoIR1 was unchanged; across the sojourn D>80%vYo-YoIR1 stayed stable in Australians but decreased largely in Bolivians. Conclusion: in sea-level natives at high altitude, match running changes track changes in high-intensity running capacity.
studies.uncertainty: Magnitude-based inferences; small n; numeric values not confirmed
studies.limitations: Very small sample (13); case-report design; youth players
studies.relevance_to_2500m_filter: Shows that visitors' absolute high-speed running loss at 3,600 m mirrors their loss of fitness capacity (i.e., players cannot compensate); same venue class as La Paz

studies.title: The impact of altitude on the sleep of young elite soccer players (ISA3600)
studies.authors: Sargent C, Schmidt WF, Aughey RJ, Bourdon PC, Soria R, Jimenez Claros JC, Garvican-Lewis LA, Buchheit M, Simpson BM, Hammond K, Kley M, Wachsmuth N, Gore CJ, Roach GD
studies.published_in: British Journal of Sports Medicine 47(Suppl 1):i86-i92; PMID 24282215; PMC3903148
studies.population: Australian U17 national team (sea-level natives)
studies.sample_size: 14 players; 19 nights (6 at 430 m, 13 at 3,600 m)
studies.design_and_measures: Wrist actigraphy every night of an 18-day camp; sleep quantity and quality
studies.measured_effects: Sleep was shorter and of poorer quality on the first night at altitude vs sea level; sleep quality returned to normal by end of week 1, but sleep quantity had still not stabilised at normal after 2 weeks. Numeric sleep-efficiency values not confirmed.
studies.uncertainty: not confirmed (statistics not visible in snippets)
studies.limitations: Actigraphy only; youth; single team; no polysomnography
studies.relevance_to_2500m_filter: First-night sleep disruption is directly relevant to the typical visitor schedule (arrive day before); extrapolation from youth to pros

studies.title: The sleep of elite athletes at sea level and high altitude: a comparison of sea-level natives and high-altitude natives (ISA3600)
studies.authors: Roach GD, Schmidt WF, Aughey RJ, Bourdon PC, Soria R, Jimenez Claros JC, Garvican-Lewis LA, Buchheit M, Simpson BM, Hammond K, Kley M, Wachsmuth N, Gore CJ, Sargent C (author order beyond first/last not fully confirmed)
studies.published_in: British Journal of Sports Medicine 47(Suppl 1):i114-i120; PMC3903309
studies.population: Australian U17 (sea-level natives, n=14) and Bolivian U20 club (altitude natives, n=12)
studies.design_and_measures: Actigraphy across 19 nights (6 at 430 m, 13 at 3,600 m); comparison of sleep quantity and quality between groups
studies.measured_effects: Australians tended to obtain more sleep than Bolivians at both locations, but Bolivians' sleep quality tended to be better than Australians' at altitude; exposure to 3,600 m induced acute and chronic disruptions to sleep efficiency of sea-level natives. Numeric values not confirmed.
studies.limitations: Actigraphy; small groups; youth
studies.relevance_to_2500m_filter: Home (altitude-native) side sleeps better at 3,600 m than sea-level visitors; mechanism for a visitor disadvantage beyond ordinary travel effects

studies.title: Predicting sickness during a 2-week soccer camp at 3600 m (ISA3600)
studies.authors: Buchheit M, Simpson BM, Schmidt WF, Aughey RJ, Soria R, Hunt RA, Garvican-Lewis LA, Pyne DB, Gore CJ, Bourdon PC
studies.published_in: British Journal of Sports Medicine 47(Suppl 1):i124-i127; PMID 24282199; PMC3903312
studies.population: Young soccer players at the ISA3600 La Paz camp (sea-level and altitude natives)
studies.design_and_measures: Time course of daily wellness and health-status markers (HR, HRV, SpO2, wellness scores) before and after sickness episodes during the camp
studies.measured_effects: Descriptive; sickness episodes occurred during the camp and were preceded by changes in wellness/health markers (specific values not confirmed)
studies.limitations: Small number of sickness cases; observational
studies.relevance_to_2500m_filter: Documents illness risk for sea-level natives at 3,600 m during a 2-week stay; marginal relevance to a short match visit

studies.title: Lower running performance and exacerbated fatigue in soccer played at 1600 m
studies.authors: Garvican LA, Hammond K, Varley MC, Gore CJ, Billaut F, Aughey RJ
studies.published_in: International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance 9(3):397-404; PMID 23751901 (epub 2013)
studies.population: Elite youth soccer players (Australian national youth team; sea-level residents)
studies.sample_size: 20 players; 1 sea-level match and 2 altitude matches (altitude days 4 and 6)
studies.altitude_range_m: sea level vs 1,600 m
studies.design_and_measures: GPS: total distance, low-velocity (0.01-4.16 m/s) and high-velocity running (4.17-10 m/s), maximal accelerations (m/min); peak and subsequent stanza to compute transient fatigue index; mean HR during submaximal running at sea level and for 10 days at altitude; magnitude-based inferences
studies.measured_effects: Total distance 'almost certainly' lower than sea level on day 4 and 'probably' reduced on day 6; HiVR 'probably' decreased on day 4; transient fatigue after peak periods 'possibly' greater at altitude; some physiological adaptation (HR) over 10 days, but match running compromised for at least 6 days. Exact % not confirmed (a 2026 consensus paper summarising this literature cites total-distance decrements of ~3-9% and high-velocity running -21%).
studies.uncertainty: Magnitude-based inference likelihoods; numeric CIs not confirmed
studies.limitations: Youth players; only 1 sea-level reference match; different opponents; low altitude (1,600 m)
studies.relevance_to_2500m_filter: Moderate-altitude study often extrapolated upward; shows decrements persist to at least day 6 even at 1,600 m, so a 1-2 day visit to 2,500-4,100 m should be at least as impaired; direct numbers cannot be transferred

studies.title: Effect of altitude on football performance: analysis of the 2010 FIFA World Cup data
studies.authors: Nassis GP
studies.published_in: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research 27(3):703-707; PMID 22648134
studies.population: National teams at the 2010 FIFA World Cup, South Africa
studies.sample_size: World Cup matches grouped by venue altitude (number of matches per band not confirmed)
studies.design_and_measures: Official tracking data: total distance, distance with/without possession, top running speed; technical indices (goals per game, goalkeeper errors leading to goals); hypothesis that distance falls above 580 m and technical skills affected via ball flight
studies.measured_effects: 3.1% lower total distance in matches at 1,200-1,400 m and 1,401-1,753 m vs sea level (p<0.05); goals per game and goalkeeper errors did not differ with altitude. Conclusion: playing above 1,200 m impaired endurance but not technical skill indices.
studies.uncertainty: p<0.05 for distance; no CI reported in snippets
studies.limitations: Team-level aggregate; teams had ~2-4 weeks in South Africa (partly acclimatised); max altitude 1,753 m; technical indices crude
studies.relevance_to_2500m_filter: Only elite senior match-tracking evidence at moderate altitude; requires large extrapolation to 2,500-4,100 m and to unacclimatised club visitors

studies.title: Moderate Altitude Affects High Intensity Running Performance in a Collegiate Women's Soccer Game
studies.authors: Bohner JD, Hoffman JR, McCormack WP, Scanlon TC, Townsend JR, Stout JR, Fragala MS, Fukuda DH
studies.published_in: Journal of Human Kinetics 47:147-154; PMID 26557199; PMC4633250
studies.population: NCAA Division I female soccer players (sea-level university, Florida)
studies.sample_size: 6 players; 2 sea-level matches vs 1 match at 1,839 m
studies.altitude_range_m: sea level vs 1,839 m
studies.design_and_measures: Retrospective 10-Hz GPS: total distance rate (m/min), high-intensity running rate (m/min), % time at HIR
studies.measured_effects: Distance rate 120.55±8.26 m/min at sea level vs 105.77±10.19 m/min at altitude (~12% lower); HIR rate 27.65±9.25 vs 25.07±7.66 m/min (~9% lower); differences reported as significant
studies.uncertainty: Reported as statistically significant; p-values/CIs not confirmed in snippets
studies.limitations: n=6, one altitude match, retrospective, opponent/match-context uncontrolled, women's collegiate level
studies.relevance_to_2500m_filter: Moderate altitude (1,839 m) and low-level population; large extrapolation to pro men at 2,500-4,100 m

studies.title: Physiological and Performance Responses to a Preseason Altitude-Training Camp in Elite Team-Sport Athletes
studies.authors: McLean BD, Buttifant D, Gore CJ, White K, Liess C, Kemp J
studies.published_in: International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance 8(4):391-399; DOI 10.1123/ijspp.8.4.391
studies.population: Elite Australian Football (AFL) players
studies.altitude_range_m: ~2,130 m (19 days) vs sea level
studies.design_and_measures: 2000 m time-trial, haemoglobin mass, intramuscular carnosine before/after a 19-day live-and-train camp; retest 4 weeks after return
studies.measured_effects: Time-trial improvement 'likely' 1.5% greater in altitude group than controls (individual responsiveness 0.8%); improvement maintained 4 weeks after return. This is an altitude-training benefit study, not an acute match-decrement study.
studies.limitations: Not soccer; measures post-camp benefits at sea level, not performance during acute arrival; no match data
studies.relevance_to_2500m_filter: Low direct relevance; shows altitude natives/acclimatised athletes gain aerobic benefit, which indirectly supports a home-side advantage mechanism; no acute-arrival decrement numbers

studies.title: Effect of altitude on football performance
studies.authors: Levine BD, Stray-Gundersen J, Mehta RD
studies.published_in: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports 18(Suppl 1):76-84; DOI 10.1111/j.1600-0838.2008.00835.x; PMID 18665955
studies.population: Narrative review (FIFA/F-MARC altitude supplement)
studies.altitude_range_m: sea level to >3,600 m (review)
studies.design_and_measures: Review of physiology and aerodynamics: reduced PO2 lowering VO2max and aerobic performance; reduced air density lowering drag (faster sprints, altered ball flight and sensorimotor skill)
studies.measured_effects: Two pathways described: hypoxia reduces VO2max, raises perceived exertion and slows recovery; lower air density facilitates high-velocity running but alters ball drag/lift, impairing sensorimotor skill. Quantitative dose-response values in the paper not confirmed from snippets.
studies.limitations: Narrative; pre-dates GPS field studies
studies.relevance_to_2500m_filter: Authoritative mechanistic basis frequently cited for high-altitude venues; no original match data

studies.title: Preparation for football competition at moderate to high altitude
studies.authors: Gore CJ, McSharry PE, Hewitt AJ, Saunders PU
studies.published_in: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports 18(Suppl 1):85-95; DOI 10.1111/j.1600-0838.2008.00836.x; PMID 18665956

studies.sample_size: not confirmed (match dataset drawn from McSharry 2007)

studies.limitations: Narrative; match-result component is observational and covered by the McSharry 2007 BMJ analysis
studies.relevance_to_2500m_filter: Authoritative FIFA-supplement source linking physiology to home advantage at >2,000 m; no GPS data

studies.title: Consensus statement on playing football at different altitude
studies.authors: Bärtsch P, Saltin B, Dvorak J
studies.published_in: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports 18(Suppl 1):96-99; DOI 10.1111/j.1600-0838.2008.00837.x

studies.design_and_measures: Consensus recommendations on acclimatisation and match scheduling by altitude zone
studies.measured_effects: Zone definitions widely reused (e.g., by Liga MX analyses); recommends acclimatisation periods increasing with altitude (specific durations not confirmed from snippets)
studies.limitations: Expert opinion
studies.relevance_to_2500m_filter: Provides the altitude-zone taxonomy: the bettor's 2,500-4,100 m band spans 'moderate' and 'high' zones where consensus recommends acclimatisation that visiting clubs normally do not get

studies.title: Position statement—altitude training for improving team-sport players' performance: current knowledge and unresolved issues
studies.authors: Girard O, Amann M, Aughey R, Billaut F, Bishop DJ, Bourdon P, Buchheit M, Chapman R, D'Hooghe M, Garvican-Lewis LA, Gore CJ, Millet GP, Roach GD, Sargent C, Saunders PU, Schmidt W, Schumacher YO (author list beyond first six not fully confirmed)
studies.published_in: British Journal of Sports Medicine 47(Suppl 1):i8-i16; DOI 10.1136/bjsports-2013-093109; PMID 24282213

studies.altitude_range_m: review
studies.design_and_measures: Synthesis of altitude effects on team-sport physical performance and altitude-training methods
studies.measured_effects: Summarises that moderate/high altitude detrimentally affects repeated-sprint ability, running endurance, distance covered and number of high-intensity sprints in matches; specific values not confirmed
studies.limitations: Consensus; largely pre-ISA3600 results
studies.relevance_to_2500m_filter: Authoritative framing; no new field numbers

studies.title: Competing at Altitude Reduces In-Match Physical Demands of Professional Soccer Players Compared With Sea Level
studies.authors: Silva H, Girard O, Monteiro J, Gasques M, Sousa A, Nakamura FY
studies.published_in: International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance 20(1):131-141 (published online 4 Dec 2024); PMID 39631388

studies.title: Effects of moderate altitude on the physical performance of elite female soccer players during an official soccer tournament
studies.authors: Kobal R, Loturco I, do Carmo EC, Cal Abad CC, Rossetti M, Saito T, Klosterhoff RR, Barroso R
studies.published_in: International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching 18(5):1558-1566; DOI 10.1177/17479541221117149
studies.population: Elite professional female soccer players (Brazilian club, sea-level based; tournament presumed 2019 Copa Libertadores Femenina in Quito, not confirmed)

studies.title: Effect of altitude on physiological performance: a statistical analysis using results of international football games
studies.authors: Patrick E. McSharry
studies.published_in: BMJ 2007;335(7633):1278-1281 (Christmas issue); PubMed PMID 18156225
studies.population: Senior men's national teams of 10 South American countries (Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Ecuador, Paraguay, Peru, Uruguay, Venezuela) playing each other
studies.altitude_range_m: Venues from sea level to ~3,600 m (La Paz); altitude differences between the two teams' home venues up to 3,695 m (Bolivia vs Brazil example)
studies.design_and_measures: Statistical models of (i) probability of a win, (ii) goals scored, (iii) goals conceded as functions of (iv) the altitude difference between each team's home venue and the opponent's; baseline home advantage read off at zero altitude difference.
studies.measured_effects: Home-win probability 0.537 when both teams are from the same altitude, rising to 0.825 at an altitude difference of 3,695 m; net goal difference shifts by roughly 0.5 goal per 1,000 m of altitude difference (high-altitude side scores more and concedes fewer as the gap widens); high-altitude teams also reported to retain an advantage when playing at low altitude (asymmetric acclimatisation).
studies.uncertainty: Altitude effect reported as significant at P<0.001; confidence intervals not visible in search results
studies.limitations: Century-long span; no explicit control for team quality/FIFA ranking confirmed (Chumacero 2009 argues the altitude variable proxies for Bolivia/Ecuador identity); international matches only; symmetric linear treatment of altitude difference; the 0.825 figure is a model extrapolation to the extreme of the range.
studies.relevance_to_2500m_filter: Direct: covers 2,600-3,600 m venues with sea-level visitors. A 2,600-3,600 m gap would imply ~1.3-1.8 net goals under the linear rule, but the estimate is unconditioned on team strength and on market prices, so it cannot be read as an edge beyond ordinary home advantage or bookmaker pricing.

studies.title: Altitude or Hot Air?
studies.authors: Rómulo A. Chumacero (Universidad de Chile)
studies.published_in: Journal of Sports Economics 10(6):619-638 (Dec 2009); earlier as MPRA Paper No. 15178
studies.population: CONMEBOL World Cup qualifying matches between South American national teams, qualifying cycles for the 1998, 2002 and 2006 World Cups
studies.sample_size: Search snippets cite '72 World Cup qualifying games'; full CONMEBOL cycles would total 270 matches, so 72 may be a subset (e.g., matches involving altitude venues) - not confirmed
studies.altitude_range_m: CONMEBOL venues: Bogotá ~2,600 m, Quito ~2,800 m, La Paz ~3,600 m vs sea-level/low venues
studies.design_and_measures: Several econometric models of match outcome and score (variants of ordered probit, with team-specific dummies, time-specific team variables and altitude variables); documents home-field advantage and other determinants of results.
studies.measured_effects: No statistical evidence that altitude is an important factor in the outcome or score once team quality (team dummies) is controlled; home-field advantage is documented; specifications that add altitude variables fit the data worse than the preferred model (Table 6).
studies.uncertainty: Coefficients and p-values not visible in search results; reported qualitatively as no significant altitude effect
studies.limitations: Small sample; altitude nearly collinear with country identity (only ~3 hosts at altitude), so team dummies absorb much of any altitude effect and the test has low power; motivated by FIFA's 2007 ban debate.
studies.relevance_to_2500m_filter: The principal null result for the exact 2,500-3,600 m band. Implies McSharry-type effects may be team-quality artefacts; for a bettor it suggests that once prices embed Bolivia/Ecuador home strength, no separately identifiable altitude premium was found.

studies.title: Altitude as handicap in rank-order football tournaments
studies.authors: Agustín Casas (Universidad Carlos III de Madrid); Yarine Fawaz (Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona)
studies.published_in: Applied Economics Letters 23(3), 2016 (doi 10.1080/13504851.2015.1061640); earlier UC3M Economics Working Paper 13-16 / RePEc we1316 (July 2013)
studies.population: CONMEBOL World Cup qualifiers; high-altitude teams (HAT; venues Bogotá, Quito, La Paz coded 1) versus low-altitude teams (LAT)
studies.sample_size: Not confirmed (number of qualifying cycles/matches not visible in search results)
studies.altitude_range_m: >2,500 m venues (Bogotá, Quito, La Paz) vs lowland venues
studies.design_and_measures: Regressions of points/outcomes on an altitude dummy and interaction terms (e.g., 'AltFelt' = LAT playing at altitude), with ordered-probit extensions; rank-order tournament framing; counterfactual qualification tables.
studies.measured_effects: (1) HAT do better against LAT than against other HAT; (2) LAT earn fewer points when visiting HAT stadiums than when playing at LAT stadiums; counterfactual: Ecuador would not have qualified for the 2002 and 2006 World Cups without the altitude advantage (2006 qualification worth at least USD 40m in FIFA payments). A descriptive figure that appeared alongside this paper (attribution not fully confirmed): in 1980-2007 qualifiers Bolivia, Colombia and Ecuador won 56%, 55% and 63% of home matches but only 6%, 24% and 9% away. Point-magnitude coefficients not extracted.
studies.limitations: Altitude dummy collinear with country identity; strength of team-quality controls not confirmed; effect magnitudes not visible; letter-length publication.
studies.relevance_to_2500m_filter: Direct for 2,500-3,600 m venues; supports an altitude effect in points beyond generic home advantage, but separation from team quality not verified from available snippets.

studies.title: Factors affecting home advantage in football World Cup qualification
studies.authors: Richard Pollard; Vasilis Armatas
studies.published_in: International Journal of Performance Analysis in Sport 17(1-2):121-135 (doi 10.1080/24748668.2017.1304031)
studies.population: National teams worldwide in the group stages of qualification for the 2006, 2010 and 2014 World Cups (balanced home-away schedules only)
studies.altitude_range_m: Worldwide venues, sea level to ~3,600 m (La Paz); altitude entered as absolute altitude of the home stadium
studies.design_and_measures: General linear model with home points as dependent variable; predictors: FIFA-ranking difference (team strength), crowd size, crowd density, distance travelled, time zones crossed, running track, altitude, confederation; model R² = 0.326.
studies.measured_effects: Overall home advantage 61.8% of points; ~69% in Africa and South America, 56% in Europe; Bolivia had the greatest home advantage of any country; after controlling for team strength, home points were significantly related to altitude of the home stadium, crowd size and time zones crossed (all p<0.05); distance travelled, running track and crowd density not significant. Authors note the large number of highland home games in South America contributed much to the altitude finding. Altitude coefficient size not extracted.
studies.uncertainty: p<0.05 for altitude; coefficient and CI not confirmed
studies.limitations: Uses absolute home-stadium altitude, not the difference relative to the visitor's base; linear points model; altitude effect largely driven by South American highland fixtures; national teams only.
studies.relevance_to_2500m_filter: Direct. Key advance over McSharry: the altitude effect survives a FIFA-ranking control, but the magnitude is unknown from available sources and the effect is entangled with Bolivia/Ecuador fixtures.

studies.title: CONMEBOL Libertadores Cup: Altitude impact on goals and results in 16 years of soccer matches
studies.authors: M. A. Cabrera-Hernández, S. A. García-Corzo, C. E. Povea-Combariza, L. J. Tafur-Tascón, H. Hurtado, J. R. Tovar-Cuevas, C. A. Mosquera-Miranda, D. F. Grijalba-González
studies.published_in: Journal of Human Sport and Exercise 18(1):34-45 (University of Alicante; RUA handle 10045/114887; ResearchGate record 2021)
studies.population: Club teams in the Copa Libertadores 2000-2015, group phase onwards, matches played at traditional home venues
studies.altitude_range_m: Club hometown altitudes from sea level to ~3,600+ m (La Paz/Potosí clubs), grouped into physiological altitude categories; a 3-category change corresponds to ~3,605 m
studies.design_and_measures: Poisson generalized linear model of goals scored by home and away teams as a function of the altitude-category change faced by the away team (ascend/descend 1-3 categories); win probabilities/odds by category change.
studies.measured_effects: Home team scores 2.62 goals on average when the away team descends 3 altitude categories, 2.01 when it descends 2, and 1.89 when it ascends 3 categories (~3,605 m); home win likelihood 5.5x (away descends 3), 2.3x (descends 2) and 2.5x (ascends 3) relative to the reference; away team more likely to lose when descending 2-3 or ascending 3 categories.
studies.uncertainty: Odds ratios reported; confidence intervals and p-values not visible in search results
studies.limitations: No team-quality control confirmed; the strong 'descend' effects (highland clubs losing at sea level) reveal confounding by the weaker quality of Bolivian/Andean clubs, so the 'ascend 3' effect is not a clean altitude estimate; coarse categories; hometown altitude may not match where squads actually train.
studies.relevance_to_2500m_filter: The only large club-match analysis found. Directly covers >2,500 m hosts (Quito, La Paz, Cusco-type clubs) with sea-level visitors: ~2.5x home-win odds and ~1.9 home goals for a ~3,600 m ascent, but not quality-adjusted or market-adjusted.

studies.title: Gasping for air: soccer players' passing behavior at high-altitude (working-paper title: Gasping for Air: Soccer Players' Performance at High-Altitude)
studies.authors: Jorge Tovar (Universidad de los Andes, Bogotá)
studies.published_in: Journal of Quantitative Analysis in Sports (De Gruyter), doi 10.1515/jqas-2014-0035; working paper: Documentos CEDE No. 11949 (2014), SSRN 2451279
studies.population: Players in Copa Libertadores club matches; away performances above vs below 2,500 m
studies.sample_size: Not confirmed (player-match observations; count not visible)
studies.altitude_range_m: Threshold 2,500 m (8,202 ft) for 'high altitude' away matches
studies.design_and_measures: Player-level comparison of total passes, passes in opposition half and successful passes when playing away above 2,500 m relative to away below 2,500 m.
studies.measured_effects: Successful-pass percentage rises by about 5.6 percentage points at high altitude, driven by each player's behaviour in his own half (more conservative play); for most indicators altitude has no impact; effects concentrated in 'risky' decisions.
studies.limitations: Process/technical metrics rather than match outcomes; Libertadores-only; away-only design; no result or goals modelling.
studies.relevance_to_2500m_filter: Mechanism evidence at exactly the 2,500 m cut-off: visiting players change behaviour (risk aversion) rather than collapsing; not a pricing edge by itself.

studies.title: The Effects of Altitude on Soccer Match Outcomes
studies.authors: Tyler Williams (described in 2011 press coverage as an MIT economics PhD candidate)
studies.published_in: Unpublished working paper (not peer reviewed); PDF hosted on a Stanford PH241 course page; year approximate (press coverage March 2011) - not confirmed
studies.population: South American international (national-team) matches
studies.altitude_range_m: 0 to ~3,600 m; exploits within-country venue variation (Colombia: Bogotá 2,550 m vs lowland; Ecuador: Quito vs Guayaquil; Bolivia: La Paz vs Santa Cruz)
studies.design_and_measures: Compares outcomes for the same team pairings hosted in the same country at different venue altitudes (fixed-effects style), removing host-country/team quality; separates 'traveling up' from 'traveling down'.
studies.measured_effects: Traveling down: no impact on outcomes. Traveling up ~2,000 m: little impact. A 4,000 m away-team ascent raises home winning percentage by about 8 points in one summary, while another passage states climbing 4,000 m 'might change winning percentage by more than 22 percent' (specification unclear). Colombia at 2,550 m: away teams have had success even for the same away team; traveling just 250 m higher to Quito generates a large negative effect for visitors, persisting at 3,600 m (La Paz). Hosts won >50% vs climbing visitors (mostly La Paz/Quito) but ~30% vs non-climbing visitors (mostly Santa Cruz/Guayaquil); roughly 4 of 8 Ecuador and 5 of 6 Bolivia home wins attributed to altitude (these figures appeared in search summaries alongside this paper; attribution not fully confirmed).
studies.limitations: Not peer reviewed; small within-country samples; Colombia may schedule its toughest opponents in Bogotá (selection effect); effect sizes differ between summaries; date and sample unverified.
studies.relevance_to_2500m_filter: Most directly designed to isolate altitude from team quality. Suggests a threshold nearer 2,800 m than 2,500 m and strong nonlinearity (no effect at Bogotá 2,550 m; large at Quito/La Paz) - argues against a flat 2,500 m rule that includes Bogotá/Toluca.

studies.title: Home advantage in European international soccer: which dimension of distance matters?
studies.authors: Nils Van Damme; Stijn Baert
studies.published_in: Economics: The Open-Access, Open-Assessment E-Journal 13 (2019-50), doi 10.5018/economics-ejournal.ja.2019-50; also IZA Discussion Paper 12143 and GLO Discussion Paper 314
studies.population: Club matches in the UEFA Champions League and UEFA Europa League
studies.altitude_range_m: European club venues (predominantly 0-1,000 m); altitude difference between home and away clubs' cities
studies.design_and_measures: Regression of home-win probability on dimensions of distance (geographic, climatic, cultural, economic prosperity, altitude difference), controlling for team-strength difference and attendance.
studies.measured_effects: Every 100 m of altitude difference in the home team's favour is associated with a +1.1 percentage-point increase in expected home-win probability; other distance dimensions not significantly associated with home advantage; home advantage larger with more spectators and when the home team is substantially stronger.
studies.uncertainty: Reported as statistically significant; CI not visible in search results
studies.limitations: European altitude range far below 2,500 m; linear extrapolation to 2,600-4,000 m differences (+29 to +44 pp) is not credible; club competition with strong team-quality heterogeneity.
studies.relevance_to_2500m_filter: Moderate/low-altitude literature that is often extrapolated to Andean venues. Shows altitude difference matters even at small gaps after quality control, but the slope cannot be scaled to >2,500 m.

studies.title: Effect of altitude on football performance: analysis of the 2010 FIFA World Cup data
studies.authors: George P. Nassis
studies.published_in: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research 27(3):703-707 (March 2013); PubMed PMID 22648134
studies.population: National teams at the 2010 FIFA World Cup (South Africa), neutral venues
studies.design_and_measures: Official match statistics: total distance covered, distance with/without possession, top speed, goals scored per game, goalkeeper errors leading to goals, compared across venue altitude bands.
studies.measured_effects: Total distance covered 3.1% lower at 1,200-1,400 m and 1,401-1,753 m than at sea level; number of goals scored per game and goalkeeper-error goals did not differ with altitude.
studies.uncertainty: Distance decrement reported as significant; goal measures non-significant; CIs not visible
studies.limitations: Neutral venues (no acclimatised home side); maximum 1,753 m; all teams equally unacclimatised; tournament sample.
studies.relevance_to_2500m_filter: Moderate-altitude evidence requiring extrapolation. Shows physical decrements without scoring effects when neither team is acclimatised - implies any 2,500 m+ result effect depends on an acclimatised home side, not altitude per se.

studies.title: Consensus statement on playing football at different altitude
studies.authors: Peter Bärtsch, Bengt Saltin, Jiri Dvorak (FIFA/F-MARC consensus group); companion pieces: Bärtsch 2008 'Football at high altitude' and Levine et al. 2008 'Effect of altitude on football performance'
studies.published_in: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports 18(Suppl 1):96-99 (doi 10.1111/j.1600-0838.2008.00837.x)
studies.population: Not applicable (expert consensus commissioned by FIFA after the 2007 altitude ban)
studies.altitude_range_m: Defines zones: near sea level 0-500 m; low 500-2,000 m; moderate 2,000-3,000 m; high 3,000-5,500 m; extreme >5,500 m
studies.design_and_measures: Consensus review of physiology, acclimatisation timing and health risks; recommendations for preparation by altitude zone.
studies.measured_effects: No new outcome data; states that performance decrements and acclimatisation requirements increase with altitude and that 2,000-3,000 m is 'moderate' and >3,000 m 'high'; underpinned FIFA's 2007-2008 rules (initial 2,500 m limit, later 2,750/3,000 m, then suspended).
studies.limitations: Not a results analysis; cites McSharry 2007 for outcome evidence.
studies.relevance_to_2500m_filter: Supplies the altitude bands used by later club studies; note that under this scheme Bogotá/Toluca/Quito (2,600-2,800 m) are 'moderate' while Cusco/Huancayo/La Paz/El Alto/Potosí (3,250-4,080 m) are 'high' - a physiologically motivated split within the bettor's 2,500-4,100 m band.

studies.title: Components of home advantage in 157 national soccer leagues worldwide
studies.authors: Richard Pollard; Miguel A. Gómez
studies.published_in: International Journal of Sport and Exercise Psychology 12(3) (doi 10.1080/1612197X.2014.888245)
studies.population: Domestic league matches in 157 national leagues
studies.sample_size: Not confirmed (number of league-seasons/matches not visible in search results)
studies.altitude_range_m: League-level indicator: whether at least two teams in the league play at high altitude
studies.design_and_measures: Home advantage measured as percentage of points won at home; multivariate model of league home advantage on geographic, cultural and structural predictors.
studies.measured_effects: Bolivia among the leagues with the highest home advantage (70-80%), with Bosnia-Herzegovina, Guatemala, Indonesia and Algeria; 'at least two teams playing at high altitude' was a significant predictor of league home advantage; pockets of high home advantage in the Andes, Balkans, West Africa and Central America.
studies.limitations: League-level aggregate; altitude is a binary league attribute rather than a per-match altitude difference; no team-quality control at match level.
studies.relevance_to_2500m_filter: Shows Andean domestic leagues (Bolivia especially) have structurally elevated baseline home advantage, which bookmakers' league-level home-advantage priors should already reflect; only indirect evidence on a premium 'beyond ordinary home advantage'.

studies.title: Worldwide regional variations in home advantage in association football
studies.authors: Richard Pollard
studies.published_in: Journal of Sports Sciences 24(3) (doi 10.1080/02640410500141836)
studies.population: Domestic top-division leagues worldwide (country count not confirmed)
studies.altitude_range_m: League-level; altitude effects noted for Bolivia and Guatemala
studies.design_and_measures: Home advantage as percentage of points won at home by region; multiple regression across 51 European countries with geography, crowd and travel variables.
studies.measured_effects: In South America home advantage is high in the Andean countries and lower elsewhere (especially Uruguay); altitude effects noted for Guatemala and Bolivia; European regression explained 76.7% of between-country variation in home advantage; territoriality suggested as main explanation for high Balkan/Andean home advantage.
studies.limitations: Descriptive regional comparison; no per-match altitude modelling; competing explanations (territoriality, crowd) not separable from altitude.
studies.relevance_to_2500m_filter: Background: establishes that Andean leagues' baseline home advantage is unusually high; any altitude filter must be benchmarked against this elevated baseline rather than a global ~60% home-points norm.

studies.title: Incidencia de las formaciones tácticas en los resultados de encuentros de futbol disputados en altitud (Incidence of tactical formations on the results of soccer matches played at altitude)
studies.authors: Oscar Homero Valencia-Aguirre, Wilson Hernando Bravo-Navarro, Lenin Esteban Loaiza-Dávila, M. H. Valencia-Cárdenas
studies.published_in: Retos 50:408-414; Dialnet record 9065165
studies.population: Ecuadorian professional league (LigaPro) matches played in cities at altitude, involving teams based at altitude and at sea level
studies.altitude_range_m: Host cities at 2,500-3,250 m
studies.design_and_measures: Instat Scout event data plus expert classification of tactical formations; effectiveness measured by points and goals for formations used by home and visiting teams at altitude.
studies.measured_effects: Effect sizes not extracted (search snippets did not show win/draw/loss percentages by formation or home advantage figures).
studies.limitations: Small sample; descriptive; no team-quality control confirmed; focus on formations rather than the altitude effect itself.
studies.relevance_to_2500m_filter: Only Ecuadorian club-league analysis found and it sits exactly in the 2,500-3,250 m band, but outcome effects could not be confirmed; would need full-text extraction.

studies.title: Playing at altitude. Performance of a Mexican professional football team at different level of altitude
studies.authors: Not confirmed from search results
studies.published_in: Apunts Sports Medicine (Elsevier), article S266650692200013X
studies.population: One Liga MX professional team, Apertura 2014 to Clausura 2018
studies.sample_size: 130 matches (6.92% near sea level, 71.53% low altitude 500-2,000 m, 21.53% moderate altitude 2,001-3,000 m)
studies.altitude_range_m: 0 to ~2,700 m (Liga MX stadiums; moderate class includes Mexico City ~2,240 m and Toluca ~2,660 m)
studies.design_and_measures: Physical performance (GPS/tracking: distances, sprints, time between sprints) and match outcome/goals for and against classified by Bärtsch et al. altitude zones.
studies.measured_effects: No statistically significant differences in performance parameters across altitude classes; no relation between altitude level and match result or goals for/against; non-significant decreases at moderate altitude attributed to fewer sprints, longer time between sprints, and playing away.
studies.limitations: Single team (home altitude not confirmed); moderate altitudes only; all Liga MX clubs regularly rotate through altitude venues so exposure is shared; small n; outcome not modelled with quality controls.
studies.relevance_to_2500m_filter: Cautions that within a league where every club routinely plays at 2,000-2,700 m, Toluca/Mexico City confer little measurable result effect versus domestic visitors; not informative about sea-level foreign visitors.

studies.title: Winning with Altitude: Evidence from College Football
studies.authors: Kyle D. Allen and colleagues (co-authors not confirmed)
studies.published_in: Sport Management Review (online 23 June 2026), doi 10.1080/14413523.2026.2689228
studies.population: NCAA Division I FBS American (gridiron) football teams - NOT association football
studies.altitude_range_m: US venues up to roughly 2,200 m; key variable is the 'altitude spread' between home venue and the opponent's native altitude
studies.design_and_measures: Regression of win probability and scoring margin on altitude spread with controls (details not confirmed).
studies.measured_effects: Home teams with a positive altitude spread have a 3.69% higher probability of winning and a 1.5-3.0 point scoring-margin advantage; advantage larger when the altitude difference is extreme.
studies.uncertainty: Reported as statistically significant; CIs not visible
studies.limitations: Different sport; maximum altitude ~2,200 m; not transferable in magnitude.
studies.relevance_to_2500m_filter: Cross-sport confirmation that altitude difference (not absolute altitude) predicts outcomes after controls, with modest effects at <=2,200 m; extrapolation to 2,500-4,100 m soccer venues is unsupported.

studies.title: How much is home advantage worth in the World Cup?
studies.authors: John Knight (johnknightstats Substack)
studies.published_in: Substack blog post, 24 April 2026 (non-peer-reviewed)
studies.population: Men's national teams; team-specific home advantage ratings fitted from results and compared with World Football Elo ratings
studies.altitude_range_m: Hosts up to La Paz 3,600 m (13,412 ft), Quito 2,850 m (9,350 ft), Mexico City 2,200 m (7,200 ft)
studies.design_and_measures: Fits a separate home-advantage rating per team from match results within an Elo-style framework.
studies.measured_effects: The three largest fitted home advantages belong to high-altitude hosts: Bolivia, Ecuador and Mexico (numeric rating values not extracted).
studies.limitations: Blog; method and data window not verified; ratings conflate altitude with other national-team home factors.
studies.relevance_to_2500m_filter: Contemporary model-based evidence that altitude hosts carry outsized team-specific home advantage; a bettor should check whether market prices already apply team-specific (not generic) home advantage before assuming value.

studies.title: Liga 1 2025: tendría 10 clubes de altura, qué pasó durante temporada de siglo XXI y cuál fue el porcentaje (Depor) / Cómo influyen la altura y los viajes en los resultados de la Liga 1 (ADFP blog)
studies.authors: Depor (Peruvian sports daily) staff; ADFP blog author not confirmed
studies.published_in: Depor.com; adfp.org.pe (non-peer-reviewed press/blog)
studies.population: Peruvian Liga 1 clubs; Lima 'big three' (Alianza Lima, Universitario, Sporting Cristal) as visitors
studies.altitude_range_m: Cusco ~3,300-3,400 m, Huancayo 3,259 m, Juliaca 3,824 m and other highland venues vs Lima sea level
studies.design_and_measures: Descriptive win percentages and home-vs-away points-per-game gaps compiled from league results.
studies.measured_effects: Lima big three win 38% of away matches at highland venues vs 48.4% at sea level (which of the listed articles carries this figure is not fully confirmed); 61.1% (11 of 18) of clubs host at altitude; largest home-away points-per-game gaps: Sport Huancayo 1.53, Garcilaso 1.47, Universitario 1.33, Moquegua 1.31, Sport Boys 1.28 (season not confirmed).

Batch 4: McSharry exact numbers (confirmed); Casas & Fawaz effect sizes (not found); Pollard & Armatas coefficients (found 2,040 games, R²=0.326; no coefficient); Williams 8%/22% (both figures appear; unresolved); UCCS referee-bias paper (not altitude-specific); Van Damme & Baert 2019 (confirmed 2,012 matches, +1.1 pp per 100 m); Pollard 2006 and Pollard & Gómez 2014 (Andean HA, Bolivia 70-80%, altitude predictor); Cryptonomist 2026 (journalism, no study); Ecuador analytics blog (no numbers); Spanish econometric search (nothing); Mexican HA econometrics (Colmex paper on social pressure; altitude handling unverified); Peru Liga 1 (press descriptives 38% vs 48.4%). Batch 5: Retos 2023 (confirmed authors, 123 matches 2020-21, 2,500-3,250 m; no effect sizes); 'Winning with Altitude' (confirmed NCAA gridiron, 14,874 games, +3.69%); Redalyc 'Llanuras' (opinion piece, not data); Chumacero model (ordered probit with team dummies); Casas & Fawaz points (no magnitudes); Williams 22% (appears in PDF text); Bärtsch consensus (confirmed zones); FunStats (blog summarising McSharry/Chumacero); xG CONMEBOL 2024-25 (nothing academic); Peru academic (nothing); bookmaker altitude pricing (nothing specific); Nassis 2013 (confirmed 64 matches, -3.1% distance, goals n.s.); 'Sánchez altitud' (only press); johnknightstats (Bolivia/Ecuador/Mexico top-3 HA). Batch 6 (partially blocked): Retos results (bibliographic only); Casas & Fawaz probit details (altitude dummy Bogotá/Quito/La Paz; Ecuador 2002 and 2006 counterfactual); remaining 10 queries (Williams sample, Pollard & Gómez altitude coefficient, Leite & Pollard 2020 JASPE, Colmex altitude control, Everardo Herrera 'estudio', Portuguese Brazilian-clubs-at-altitude, Bolivian economics 2021-24, Ecuador/Bolivia theses, McSharry ResearchGate variant title, PIT Journal) were refused by the budget cap.
science.gaps: (1) No peer-reviewed match-outcome analysis of the Bolivian, Peruvian or Colombian domestic leagues at altitude was found; the only club-league items are the Ecuadorian Retos 2023 paper (effects not extracted) and a single-team Liga MX study. (2) No study specifically tests whether bookmaker odds price altitude (no betting_market study with altitude found; Bruce Lezana 2026 JSE uses EPL data and altitude content is unconfirmed; the 'academic study included altitude difference as a control in implicit-probability analysis' claim surfaced in a search summary could not be traced to a citable paper). (3) Exact altitude coefficients/CIs for Pollard & Armatas 2017, Casas & Fawaz 2016 and Van Damme & Baert 2019, and the sample size for Casas & Fawaz, Williams and Tovar, were not visible. (4) Chumacero's '72 games' sample could not be reconciled with 270 full-cycle CONMEBOL matches. (5) Williams' effect size is reported inconsistently (~8 pts vs '>22%') and the paper's date/sample are unverified. (6) No replication or formal rebuttal of Chumacero 2009 was located; the McSharry-vs-Chumacero disagreement remains unresolved in the literature found. (7) No Copa Sudamericana or Copa América altitude analysis found. (8) No study distinguishes visitors' training elevation from hometown altitude, and none uses the parent question's exact '>2,500 m above the visitor's usual elevation' definition; Williams' within-country evidence suggests Bogotá (~2,600 m) behaves differently from Quito/La Paz, so a flat 2,500 m cut-off is not supported by the results-based literature. (9) 'Kraus' and 'Sanchez' altitude-results papers named in the brief could not be identified (the only 'Sanchez' hit is a Peruvian betting blog, rsanchez.pe). (10) Ten planned follow-up queries (Pollard & Gómez altitude coefficient, Leite & Pollard 2020 JASPE, Colmex Mexican HA paper altitude control, Portuguese Brazilian-club analyses, Ecuador/Bolivia theses, McSharry ResearchGate variant, PIT Journal UNC) were blocked by the search budget and remain unverified.
